title: The rehatnamas
hookLine: codes of conduct linked to the Tenth Guru's time, written down by Sikhs after him

lines: HOW WE WANT TO LIVE, WRITTEN DOWN.
CODES OF HOW A SIKH SHOULD LIVE.
cards: A family keeps a list on the fridge. Shoes off at the door. Nobody eats until everyone sits.
Say thank you to whoever cooked. Nobody voted on it, exactly. It grew out of how the family wanted to live, and somebody finally wrote it down.
After the Tenth Guru, Sikhs wrote down lists like that, on a much larger scale: what to do at dawn, how to treat a guest, what to give, what to avoid.

teach.h: REHAT, A WAY OF LIVING. NAMA, A WRITING.
teach.b: The word is rehatnama. Rehat is a way of living, a discipline kept day after day. Nama is a written piece, a letter or a record.
Together: a written code for living. Tradition links these codes to the circle around Guru Gobind Singh.
Some carry the names of Sikhs remembered as close to him; one is linked with Bhai Nand Lal, remembered as a poet of the Guru's court.

teach.h: WRITTEN DOWN AFTER THE GURU'S TIME.
teach.b: They were written down after the Guru's time, and that matters for how they're read. They are not scripture. They sit beside the Guru Granth Sahib, not inside it.
What do they hold? Mostly ordinary things, which is the point. Rise early.
Remember the Name. Bathe and recite the morning prayers. Share what you earn.
Keep the hair uncut. Treat the Guru's word with honor. For the Sikhs who wrote them, faith was not only an inner feeling.

teach.h: A SHAPE FOR THE WHOLE DAY.
teach.b: It was a shape for the whole day. Here's the honest part. The rehatnamas don't all say the same thing.
They differ in detail, and some hold lines that later Sikhs questioned or set aside.

teach.h: THEY DIFFER; A SHARED CODE CAME LATER.
teach.b: Scholars and Sikh bodies have read them side by side, and out of that long conversation came a shared code you'll meet later on the path, the Sikh Rehat Maryada.
So a rehatnama is a window, not a final word: early Sikhs putting the Gurus' teaching into daily life, written down by people who cared enough to try.

how: Sikh historians and teachers read the rehatnamas as early records of Sikh discipline; for daily practice, gurdwaras and Sikh families follow the Sikh Rehat Maryada, a shared code drawn up later.

games.q: you find an old rehatnama with a line that clashes with another code. how do Sikh readers handle it?

games.why: scholars and Sikh bodies read them carefully together. out of that conversation came the shared Sikh Rehat Maryada.

practice: Think about how you actually want your days to go, not how you think you ought to want them, and find one plain line for your own code, like phone down at the table, or answer kindly before answering fast.
Keep it short enough to fit on a fridge, write it down if you have paper, and sit with it to see whether it still fits.

wordCard.voice: Rehatnama. A written code of Sikh living, linked by tradition to the Tenth Guru's circle and written down after him. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: rehat, a way of living, and nama, a written piece: a written code of conduct.

carryVoice: Your line: a code for living. Faith with a shape you can see, from dawn on. See you tomorrow.
